## Guided Tutorial 7.1: Forecasting Revenue and Testing the Forecast

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will prepare the revenue forecast the controller asked for. You will build a monthly revenue series from the InvoiceLines Table, measure what moves with it using correlation, fit a trend with the Data Analysis ToolPak, and examine what drives the trend. You will then backtest three forecasting methods on the fourth quarter of 2026, the most recent quarter with actual results, and use the best one to forecast the first quarter of 2027 with a range.

**Prerequisites.** You need the analysis workbook from Chapter 6, with the InvoiceLines Table, and the Analysis ToolPak loaded, as described earlier in this chapter.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Build the monthly revenue series.** EDATE, used below, returns the date a given number of months after a start date, so each row of the series starts one month after the row above it.

a. Add a worksheet named `Forecast`, and type the headings `Month`, `MonthIndex`, and `Revenue` in A1:C1.
b. Type `2024-01-01` in A2.
c. In A3, enter `=EDATE(A2,1)`, and fill it down to A37, which shows December 2026.
d. Format A2:A37 with the custom number format `mmm yyyy`.
e. Type `1` in B2, enter `=B2+1` in B3, and fill it down to B37.
f. In C2, enter this formula, and fill it down to C37:

   ```
   =SUMIFS(InvoiceLines[LineTotal],InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate],">="&A2,InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate],"<"&EDATE(A2,1))
   ```

g. Type `Control total` in A38, and enter `=SUM(C2:C37)-SUM(InvoiceLines[LineTotal])` in C38.

C38 is zero: every invoice line falls in one of the thirty-six months, so the series accounts for all of the revenue.

**Step 2. Chart the series.** A line chart suits a measure over time, as the section on charting in Chapter 6 explained.

a. Select A1:A37, hold Ctrl, and select C1:C37.
b. Choose **Insert > Insert Line or Area Chart > Line with Markers**.

Almost every month falls within a narrow band, but the first month is far below the rest. January 2024 is the start-up month of the data, in which Charles River issued only about half as many invoices as in a normal month. @fig-07-01 shows the same series with the trend lines you will fit later.

**Step 3. Measure what moves with revenue.** Revenue rises when more customers buy or when each purchase is larger, so a correlation matrix shows which of the two moves with it.

a. Type the headings `Customers` and `AverageLine` in D1:E1.
b. In D2, enter this formula, which counts the different customers invoiced in the month, and fill it down to D37. FILTER keeps the month's rows, multiplying the two conditions so that a row must meet both, and UNIQUE removes the repeated customer IDs before COUNTA counts them.

   ```
   =COUNTA(UNIQUE(FILTER(InvoiceLines[CustomerID],(InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate]>=A2)*(InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate]<EDATE(A2,1)))))
   ```

c. In E2, enter this formula, the average line total of the month, and fill it down to E37:

   ```
   =AVERAGEIFS(InvoiceLines[LineTotal],InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate],">="&A2,InvoiceLines[InvoiceDate],"<"&EDATE(A2,1))
   ```

d. Choose **Data > Data Analysis**, select **Correlation**, and click **OK**.
e. Enter `$C$1:$E$37` as the **Input Range**, and check **Labels in first row**.
f. Choose **Output Range**, enter `$G$1`, and click **OK**.
g. Run the tool again with `$C$3:$E$37` as the **Input Range**, **Labels in first row** cleared, and `$G$7` as the **Output Range**. Without the headings, Excel labels the three variables Column 1, Column 2, and Column 3.

With all thirty-six months, in G1:J4, revenue is strongly correlated with the number of customers and only weakly with the average line. Without January 2024, in G7:J10, the order reverses: the correlation with customers is much weaker, and the average line becomes the stronger partner. One start-up month with few customers made the number of customers look like the driver of revenue.

**Step 4. Fit a trend to all thirty-six months.**

a. Choose **Data > Data Analysis**, select **Regression**, and click **OK**.
b. Enter `$C$1:$C$37` as the **Input Y Range** and `$B$1:$B$37` as the **Input X Range**, and check **Labels**.
c. Choose **New Worksheet Ply**, and type `Trend36`.
d. Check **Residuals** and **Residual Plots**, and click **OK**.
e. On the Trend36 worksheet, read R Square, the MonthIndex coefficient, and its P-value.

R Square is low: the month index explains only about a sixth of the variation in monthly revenue. Yet the slope is positive and its p-value is below 0.05, so the trend is statistically significant. The residual plot shows why. One residual, January 2024's, lies far below all the others, and a line that must pass near it tilts upward. @fig-07-02 shows the output.

**Step 5. Fit the trend again without the start-up month.**

a. Run the Regression tool again, with `$C$3:$C$37` as the **Input Y Range** and `$B$3:$B$37` as the **Input X Range**.
b. Clear the **Labels** check box, because the ranges no longer start with the headings.
c. Place the output on a new worksheet ply named `Trend35`.
d. Compare R Square, the slope, and its p-value with those on Trend36.

Without January 2024, R Square falls further, the slope shrinks to about half its former size, and its p-value rises above 0.05. The upward trend was the start-up month, not a pattern in the business. Monthly revenue has fluctuated around a stable level since February 2024.

**Step 6. Backtest three forecasts of the fourth quarter of 2026.** Each method is fitted to February 2024 through September 2026, rows 3 to 34, as if the forecast had been prepared at the end of September.

a. Type the headings `Method`, `Oct 2026`, `Nov 2026`, `Dec 2026`, `Quarter`, `Error`, and `Monthly error` in A40:G40.
b. Type the labels `Actual`, `Trend`, `Mean`, and `Same quarter last year` in A41:A44.
c. In B41:D41, enter `=C35`, `=C36`, and `=C37`, the actual revenue of the three months.
d. In B42, enter the trend forecast for October, which is MonthIndex 34:

   ```
   =FORECAST.LINEAR($B35,$C$3:$C$34,$B$3:$B$34)
   ```

   In C42 and D42, enter the same formula with `$B36` and `$B37`.
e. In B43:D43, enter `=AVERAGE($C$3:$C$34)`, the mean of the fitted months.
f. In B44:D44, enter `=C23`, `=C24`, and `=C25`, the same months of 2025.

Rows 42 to 44 now hold each method's forecast of the three months, made only from the months before October 2026, next to the actual revenue in row 41.

**Step 7. Measure the forecast errors.**

a. In E41, enter `=SUM(B41:D41)`, and copy it to E42:E44.
b. In F42, enter `=E42/$E$41-1`, the error of the quarter's total, and copy it to F43:F44.
c. In G42, enter `=AVERAGE(ABS(B42:D42-$B$41:$D$41)/$B$41:$D$41)`, the mean absolute percentage error of the three months, and copy it to G43:G44.
d. Format F42:G44 as percentages with two decimals.

The trend forecast overshoots the quarter by several percent, because it extends a slope that the business does not have. The mean misses the quarter by a small fraction of a percent and has the smallest monthly errors. The same quarter of last year comes close on the quarter's total, but only because its large monthly errors offset one another. @fig-07-03 shows the comparison. The simplest method is the best of the three here, which is the reason to test benchmarks before trusting a more elaborate forecast.

![Backtesting Three Forecasts of the Fourth Quarter of 2026.](/visuals/svg/fig-07-03-forecast-backtest.svg){#fig-07-03 fig-alt="A mock of the backtest area of the Forecast worksheet. For October, November, and December 2026 and the whole quarter, it shows the actual revenue and the forecasts of three methods: a trend from FORECAST.LINEAR, the mean of February 2024 to September 2026, and the same quarter of the previous year. The error columns, outlined, show that the trend overshoots the quarter by several percent, the mean is almost exactly right, and the same quarter last year is close on the total but has the largest monthly errors."}

**Step 8. Forecast the first quarter of 2027 with a range.**

a. Type `Forecast, 2027 Q1` in A47, and enter `=3*AVERAGE(C3:C37)` in B47, which applies the mean method to every month after the start-up month.
b. Type `Low` in A48 and `High` in A49.
c. Enter `=B47*(1-G43)` in B48 and `=B47*(1+G43)` in B49, a range based on the mean method's monthly error in the backtest.

The forecast is close to the revenue of the last few quarters, and the range extends a few percent on either side of it.

**Step 9. Document the forecast.**

a. On the **Documentation** worksheet, add the Forecast, Trend36, and Trend35 worksheets to the Worksheets entry.
b. Add a `Forecast` entry that records the method, the months it uses, the reason January 2024 is excluded, the backtest results, and the range.
c. Save the workbook.

A reviewer can now see how the forecast was made and why the simplest of the methods was chosen.

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- C38 is zero, so the monthly series contains all of the revenue;
- without January 2024, revenue correlates more closely with the average line than with the number of customers;
- the trend's slope is significant with January 2024 and not significant without it;
- the mean method has the smallest errors in the backtest;
- the forecast for the first quarter of 2027 is stated with a low and a high value.

The controller now has a forecast she can defend. It is not the most sophisticated method you could build, but it is the one that performed best on the most recent quarter with an answer, and its range tells her how much to rely on it.
